Baby & Child

Hypoplastic left heart syndrome: symptoms, circulation and care

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is a serious heart difference present at birth. The left side is too underdeveloped to supply the body effectively. A newborn may initially seem well, but needs specialist care because circulation can fail as normal fetal connections change after birth.

What is underdeveloped in HLHS?

The left ventricle, the main pumping chamber for the body, is very small. The mitral and aortic valves may be small or closed, and the ascending aorta may also be narrow. The exact combination varies.

Normally, the right heart sends blood to the lungs and the left heart sends oxygen-rich blood through the aorta to the body. In HLHS, the right ventricle must support both routes; it cannot simply replace a normal two-pump circulation without treatment.

Two different connections matter

The ductus arteriosus is a blood vessel connecting the pulmonary artery to the aorta. The foramen ovale, or another atrial opening, connects the left and right upper chambers. These are different structures, not two names for the same opening.

Blood returning from the lungs must cross from the left atrium to the right atrium. The right ventricle pumps mixed blood toward the lungs and, through the ductus, the body. Duct closure can sharply reduce body blood flow. A restrictive or closed atrial opening creates an additional serious obstruction.

Symptoms and when to seek emergency help

Some babies become ill immediately; others worsen over the first days. Signs include blue, grey or unusually pale skin or lips, rapid or difficult breathing, poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, cold hands or feet and weak pulses. A heart murmur can be faint or absent.

Call emergency services immediately for difficult or very fast breathing, blue or grey colour or unusually pale or blotchy skin, cold or clammy skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a baby who is floppy, unresponsive or hard to wake. Shock can develop rapidly; do not wait for every sign, a routine appointment or an app reading.

Causes, family history and prevention

HLHS develops while the fetal heart forms. Most families are not given a single explanation, and parents usually have not caused it. Genetic or chromosome differences contribute in some children; a family history of HLHS or another congenital heart defect can increase recurrence risk.

There is no proven way to prevent every case. A genetics professional and congenital-heart specialist can review the family history, discuss appropriate testing and estimate individual recurrence risk. Counseling and fetal heart assessment can guide choices and planning, but cannot promise an unaffected future baby.

Diagnosis and planning the birth

A pregnancy ultrasound may raise concern; a fetal echocardiogram gives a detailed view of heart structure and blood flow. A prenatal diagnosis allows the maternity and cardiac teams to plan delivery where the newborn can be assessed and stabilized promptly.

After birth, echocardiography defines the anatomy and function. Examination, oxygen measurements and other selected tests add information. A reassuring earlier scan, newborn oxygen screen or lack of a murmur does not justify ignoring a sick baby.

Immediate stabilization is specialist care

In hospital, an infusion of prostaglandin can keep the ductus arteriosus open while the team plans intervention. It keeps that vessel open; it does not open a restrictive atrial septum. A baby with inadequate atrial communication may need an urgent separate procedure.

Care also balances blood flow to the body and lungs, supports breathing and checks organ function. Oxygen, ventilation, medicines and feeding are managed individually by the cardiac team. These are not treatments to start, change or stop at home.

Surgery, hybrid treatment and transplant

A common pathway is staged palliation: a Norwood operation in the newborn period, then a Glenn and later a Fontan procedure. These reroute circulation so the right ventricle supplies the body and returning blood reaches the lungs more directly. Timing and technique depend on the child, rather than a fixed schedule for everyone.

Selected babies have a hybrid approach combining catheter procedures and surgery, such as a ductal stent and pulmonary-artery bands. Transplant may be considered in some circumstances and requires lifelong anti-rejection treatment. All options carry risks. When intervention cannot offer an acceptable pathway, the team can discuss comfort-focused care and family support.

Long-term complications and development

Treatment has improved survival, but it does not create a normal two-ventricle heart or remove lifelong risk. Possible problems include reduced exercise tolerance, abnormal rhythms, weakened heart function, fluid accumulation, blood clots and further procedures or transplant. Risks differ between children.

Feeding difficulty and poor growth need early support; some babies need enriched feeds or a feeding tube under a prescribed plan. Developmental assessment can identify needs for therapy and learning support. Later care also monitors other organs, including the liver, and continues with an adult congenital-heart team.

A practical follow-up plan for families

Between operations, ask for written medicine and feeding instructions, a contact number available outside clinic hours and clear warning thresholds. If the cardiac team prescribes home weight or oxygen monitoring, learn the equipment and the exact response plan; do not invent a target or change medicines from a reading alone.

Ask about safe activity, vaccinations, dental care and whether any procedures need special precautions. Seek advice promptly for new symptoms, poorer feeding or growth, or a change from the child’s usual condition. Emergency signs still require emergency services, even when the cardiac clinic is already involved.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC information dated January 2026 and AHA information reviewed July 2026 describe critical newborn circulation and lifelong care. Specialist hospital guidance distinguishes the ductus from atrial communication and supports an individualized treatment pathway.

AHA genetic-counseling information reviewed September 2026 supports family-specific assessment, not guaranteed prevention. NHS emergency guidance reviewed August 2026 supports acting immediately on serious newborn warning signs.

The AHA interstage-monitoring statement was published in 2020; its practical framework supports training and a written response plan. Hospital resources without a displayed date are not presented as newly issued 2026 guidelines.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help keep appointments, prescribed feeding and medicine plans, and questions together. It cannot assess circulation, set oxygen targets or decide whether a baby is stable; warning signs override tracking.

When to seek help

Seek immediate emergency help for breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour or unusually pale or blotchy skin, cold or clammy skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a baby who is floppy, unresponsive or hard to wake. Do not delay care to log symptoms, and do not adjust cardiac medicines, oxygen or feeds without the treating team’s plan.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • HLHS is critical congenital heart disease; appearing well at birth does not remove the need for a cardiac plan.
  • The ductus joins two arteries; the atrial opening is separate, and either pathway can become dangerously restricted.
  • Operations improve circulation but are palliation, with individualized risks and lifelong follow-up.
  • Breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour or unusually pale or blotchy skin, cold or clammy skin or loss of consciousness needs immediate emergency help.

Frequently asked questions

What causes HLHS?

It develops during fetal heart formation. The precise cause is often unknown; some cases involve genetic or chromosome differences. Most parents have not done anything to cause it.

What complications can HLHS cause?

Without effective intervention it is life-threatening. After treatment, possible complications include rhythm problems, reduced heart function or exercise tolerance, fluid buildup, clots, feeding or developmental difficulties and further procedures. An individual outlook requires specialist assessment.

Does family history increase the risk?

It can. The recurrence risk depends on the particular defect, family history and any identified genetic cause; one percentage does not fit every family. Genetic counseling can help.

Can HLHS be prevented?

No method guarantees prevention. Preconception or pregnancy counseling can discuss testing and fetal echocardiography and support informed planning, without promising an unaffected baby.

Can a baby with HLHS seem well at first?

Yes. Symptoms may worsen as the ductus closes over the first days, although some babies are severely ill immediately. Do not wait for symptoms if a diagnosis is already known.

Does prostaglandin keep both openings open?

No. It keeps the ductus arteriosus open. An inadequate opening between the atria is a different problem and may require an urgent procedure.

Do the operations cure HLHS?

No. Staged or hybrid procedures improve blood flow but do not create a normal two-ventricle circulation. Lifelong congenital-heart care is needed; transplant has its own long-term treatment requirements.

Which symptoms cannot wait for a routine appointment?

Difficult or very fast breathing, blue or grey colour or unusually pale or blotchy skin, cold or clammy skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a floppy, unresponsive or hard-to-wake baby require immediate emergency help. Not all signs need to be present.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
